meta.title: Intervals: The Distance Between Notes
meta.summary: Musicians hear distances, not notes. Here is how to count them on a fretboard.

spans.text: Sing the first two notes of
Somewhere Over the Rainbow
and you have sung an octave — in whatever key you happened to start in. What you recognised was not the notes. It was the
distance
between them. That distance is an interval, and it is the unit everything else is built from.
Counting in half steps

A guitar makes intervals unusually easy to count: one fret is one half step, two frets is a whole step, and that is all the arithmetic there is. Every interval gets a number — how many letter names it spans — and a
quality
that nudges it by a fret.

rows.text: the shadow in every sad chord
the brightness in every happy one

spans.text: Why fourths and fifths feel like furniture
The perfect fifth — seven frets — is the most stable interval there is after the octave. A
power chord
is nothing but a root and its fifth, which is why it fits over a major or a minor progression without complaint: it has no third, so it takes no side.
The perfect fourth — five frets — is why standard tuning is shaped the way it is. Strings 6 to 3 are stacked in fourths, and so are strings 2 to 1.
The one exception is the gap between strings 3 and 2, which is a
major third
. That single irregularity is why so many chord and scale shapes look symmetrical until they cross the B string, and then shift by a fret.
A scale is a pattern of intervals
Once distance is the unit, a scale stops being seven note names and becomes one shape. The major scale is
half steps from its root, on any root, on any string. Move one of those numbers and you change the mood without leaving the key.
Here is the smallest possible edit: lower the seventh by one fret. Major becomes
Mixolydian
— six identical tones and one that moved.
Play them back to back. Major leans hard toward home on its seventh note; Mixolydian shrugs and keeps going. One fret, and a scale that resolves becomes a scale that grooves.
Train the distance, not the note

items.text: Pick a fret at random, then find the note seven frets up
naming either one. You are learning the shape of a fifth, not a pair of letters.
Hum the top note of an interval before you play it. Being wrong is the useful part.
When a riff catches your ear, count the frets between its first two notes and write the number down.

spans.text: The most consequential interval of all is the third — it decides whether a chord is happy or sad. That one gets its own article:
Major vs Minor
Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths come in
major
and
minor
flavours, one fret apart. Fourths, fifths and octaves are called
perfect
instead — they have no major or minor form, only augmented and diminished versions a fret either side.
